Voat is a hit or miss phenomenon. We want to see the platform succeed but there are some challenges facing it.

Very many of us are refugees from the plethora of online communities that have failed due to administrative and moderation missteps.

I've been around since the old builtin board days when you used an acoustic coupler to get online. I've learned a great many things about social communities in a digital space since then.

There is ultimately a fatal flaw with any system, human behavior. We have safe-space crybabies, chaotic anarchists, and a spectrum in, around, and between those extremes. Humans are diverse and will never coexist without disagreement and conflict.

There is no universally valid perspective or opinion. There is no common sense. No consensus. Only in a regime of intimidation and fear can any perspective become ubiquitous.

Voat is trumpeted as a field for those disenfranchised by censorship to speak freely.

We have our Amaleks, our fat people haters, our feminist whores, the pedophiles, and much much more.

People push the limits, test one another, all an effort to see just how free they are to express who they are.

Human desire for freedom is innate. Human emotions demand expression and in an oppressed society the freedom to express emotions are denied to those who do not possess the emotions conducive to their repression.

We stand at a cross road on Voat. Site traffic is on the decline as people begin to pour all of their pent up frustrations out onto its subverses. Racism is common, fat shaming, woman hating, and much more are all noticeably visible in every corner of the site.

Above all this is a testament to success of this platform to deliver users a venue to express them selves with out fear of reprisal. But it's not yet fully realized.

We have turned our conflict with oppression inwards on our own communities. Subs curated by one group being attacked by another. Chaos striking at order. Order striking at chaos. We have mods who over step and users who react in extremes. We have cowards that hide behind convenient truths and votes that silence inconvenient opinions.

We are dysfunctional. It's endearing to a lover of chaos like my self. Frustrating to proponents of order.

Where do we find a balance that lets us each find harmony?

Let us consider points of contention:

Subs need curating for consumers to be able to find the content they seek. Content creators are desperately opposed to the destruction of the content they create and the voice they speak with. We often point at users like @eggnogg and say "Look what that shift bastard did! He wiped out a conversation with 146 participants because of a stupid rule that half of the sites users disagree with."

In the past users could rear up and maliciously silence a misbehaving moderator with a furry of downvoats. This being what silenced @she during the shebakle. With recent site changes the power of content consumers to protest with actions was stripped from them. Downvoating a user to oblivion is no longer possible. This is good in part because it would have been abused in many ways when debate could resolve a conflict in its stead.

Sadly the downstream result is an emboldened moderator class that is all but immune to public outcry for missteps.

Let us consider now that a other means exist to solve the dangers of future crimes by mobs without restricting the ability of content consumers and content contributors to defend the integrity of the flow of information.

The two powers moderator class hold over the creator and consumer classes of our society are the abilities to delete comments and delete posts. We have seen racist comments removed for risking offense to users who are traumatized by others outbursts of emotional strife and we have seen the order driven moderator class silence while debates because they fall outside of their sense of what belongs in a category.

TL;DR;

How do such situations find resolution without preventing curators from maintaining communities while not attacking the very users of the communities they curate?

It's simple, provide a soft delete feature that allows users to opt-out of a specific moderators curation.

For each user who seeks to be a buffer between the free flow of information and the consumer of information we provide a set of tools to flag content they wish to remove from the view of others. If a user wishes to subscribe to the narrowed view of information the curator creates, they may do so, for those who wish to have a fuller view of the raw feed of user contributed content, they may disable the moderated view of content.

An enumerated set of flags can be used to specify the degree of moderation from "spam" to "offensive" so that users may choose how narrowed their window into the world is.

Well, most economists oppose how the dole is given out, while not opposing the idea of aid itself. Even Milton Friedman supported the idea of financial aid.

The problem with the "dole" as it is traditionally implemented, is that once you get a job, suddenly you lose the entire sum of the financial aid. Because of this "bump" no one is financially incentivised to seek low-paying work. This specific problem has nothing to do with Islam, btw. Every poor person has this problem: once you get a job, you often (depending on laws) lose the entirety of financial assistance, and it then makes no financial sense to say start a minimum wage job.

And there is a solution to this. The solution is to either give people a flat amount of financial aid regardless of circumstances, which is the most elegant solution. That's known as a UBI (universal basic income). Or, to adopt a policy of gradualism with regard to financial aid, and to avoid withholding all the aid at some arbitrary point. That's something Milton Friedman, a conservative economist, proposes in NIT.

The idea is simple: when you get a job, you should experience an increase in your finances and not a decrease, no matter what that job is, and no matter what kind of dole you had before. That's not so hard to implement. This will financially incentivize people to get off the dole. But the way we implement dole now, there is a point where you lose money by getting a job. That's a bad incentive structure.
